title: Rostov falls, for a week
pull: The gateway to the Caucasus, held eight days

facts.text: On 21 November 1941, German troops of General Ewald von Kleist's First Panzer Army took Rostov on Don, the big Soviet city on the Don River near the Sea of Azov.
Rostov was a rail junction and river port that opened the way to the Caucasus and its oil. The assault on the city had begun on 17 November.
Kleist's tanks had driven all the way from Kiev. The autumn rains turned roads to mud, and his leading units did not reach the outskirts of Rostov until mid November.

Then winter came in full force. The Germans were short of food, fuel, ammunition, vehicles, spare parts and winter clothing, and Kleist warned that his tanks were not working well in the freezing weather and that his left flank was open.
Field Marshal Gerd von Rundstedt, commanding Army Group South, had already urged in early November that his armies halt and dig in for the winter. He was overruled.
On 27 November the Soviet 37th Army struck the panzer spearhead from the north and threatened to cut it off.
On 28 November Rundstedt allowed Kleist to pull out of Rostov to a line on the Mius River, about 70 kilometers west. The Red Army was back in the city by 28 to 29 November; sources differ on the day.
Hitler ordered Rostov held. Rundstedt replied: "It is madness to attempt to hold. In the first place the troops cannot do it and in the second place if they do not retreat they will be destroyed."

On 1 December 1941 Hitler dismissed Rundstedt and gave Army Group South to Field Marshal Walther von Reichenau. Reichenau saw at once that Rundstedt was right, and Hitler soon allowed the withdrawal to the Mius.
It was the first significant German withdrawal of the war, and one of the first signs that the drive into the Soviet Union had run out of strength.
The Germans came back. They took Rostov again in July 1942 and held it until 14 February 1943.

sources.title: Dwight Jon Zimmerman, The Nazi Blame Game: The Fall of Ernst Udet and Gerd von Rundstedt, Defense Media Network

photoNote: German Panzer III and other tanks roll down a smoke filled street past a burning Soviet truck. Original caption 'Panzerdurchbruch nach Shitomir. PK-Grimm' (tank breakthrough to Zhitomir): Zhitomir, Ukraine, July 1941, during the advance of Kleist's Panzer Group 1 (it became the First Panzer Army in October 1941). Not Rostov and not November: it shows the same panzer army months earlier, at the start of the drive that ended at Rostov. German Army propaganda company photo, NARA 242-GAV-II-176 (item record naId 221952064; image from Album 2, naId 352357716, page 176, left photo), National Archives Collection of Foreign Records Seized, use Unrestricted. Cropped from the album page (left print only), 1920 x 1369. No SS insignia visible; no people in focus. I found no captured German photo of Rostov itself in NARA's digitized 242 series.
photoCredit: German tanks advance through Zhitomir, Ukraine, July 1941. German Army propaganda company photo, NARA 242-GAV-II-176, public domain.

declassified.fact: On 3 December Hitler flew to the army group's headquarters at Poltava to see for himself. After hearing his generals out, he called the whole affair a misunderstanding and suggested Rundstedt take some leave. Rundstedt left Poltava on 5 December and never returned to the Russian front.

body:
Field Marshal Gerd von Rundstedt told Hitler it was madness to try to hold the city. Days later he was dismissed.

21 November 1941. Troops of Ewald von Kleist's First Panzer Army took Rostov on Don, the rail junction and river port that opened the way to the Caucasus and its oil. They had driven all the way from Kiev through the autumn mud, and now winter had come. The panzer army was short of food, fuel, spare parts and winter clothing, and its left flank hung open.

On 27 November the Soviet 37th Army struck that flank. Rundstedt let Kleist pull back to the Mius River. Hitler ordered Rostov held and on 1 December replaced Rundstedt, whose successor soon reached the same conclusion.

It was the first significant German withdrawal of the war.

Field Marshal Gerd von Rundstedt told Hitler it was madness to try to hold the city. Days later he was dismissed.

21 November 1941. The First Panzer Army took Rostov on Don, the gateway to the Caucasus. Eight days later, short of fuel and winter clothing and struck in the flank, it pulled out: the first significant German withdrawal of the war.
